1.s: The risen Jesus tells his followers to wait for the Holy Spirit: “You will be witnesses… to the uttermost parts of the earth.” He is taken up into heaven. Matthias replaces Judas.
1.d: Luke’s Gospel told of Jesus’ work on earth; Acts tells of the Holy Spirit’s work through his followers [[bsn:Acts 1:1-11]]. Acts 1:8 maps the book: the good news goes out from Jerusalem and Judea, to Samaria, and on to the ends of the earth [[tosn:Acts 1:8]].

2.s: At Pentecost the Spirit comes like wind and fire, and the disciples speak in other languages. Peter preaches, and three thousand believe. The believers share everything.
2.d: Peter quotes Joel 2:28–32: in the last days God pours out his Spirit on young and old, men and women [[tosn:Acts 2:17-21]]. Pentecost marks the beginning of the Christian church [[tosn:Acts 2:14-36]]. The new community devoted itself to the apostles’ teaching, fellowship, the breaking of bread and prayer [[bible:Acts 2:42]] [[tosn:Acts 2:42-47]].

3.s: Peter and John heal a man lame from birth at the temple gate: “What I have, that I give you.” Peter preaches about Jesus, the prophet like Moses.
3.d: “I have no silver or gold” [[bible:Acts 3:6]]: the healing is done in the name of Jesus, which shows who he is and his power to heal [[tosn:Acts 3:6]], just as Luke’s Gospel tells of Jesus healing [[bsn:Acts 3:1-10]].

4.s: Peter and John are arrested and boldly tell the council, “There is salvation in no one else.” The believers pray, the place shakes, and they share possessions.
4.d: The leaders opposed Peter and John as they had opposed Jesus [[bsn:Acts 4:1-22]], and saw that they were “unlearned and ignorant men” who “had been with Jesus” [[bible:Acts 4:13]]. Barnabas is an example of generous, unselfish giving [[tosn:Acts 4:36-37]].

5.s: Ananias and Sapphira lie about a gift and die. The apostles are arrested, freed by an angel, and say, “We must obey God rather than men.” Gamaliel advises caution.
5.d: Gamaliel was a respected Pharisee and teacher of the law [[tosn:Acts 5:34]], the rabbi Paul studied under when he was young [[tbd:007:Gamaliel]] [[bible:Acts 22:3]]. The apostles left “rejoicing that they were counted worthy to suffer dishonor for Jesus’ name” [[bible:Acts 5:41]].

6.s: Seven men, including Stephen, are chosen to care for neglected Greek-speaking widows. Stephen is arrested.
6.d: Greek-speaking widows were being overlooked [[tosn:Acts 6:1]]. The seven chosen to care for them all have Greek names, and they are sometimes called the first deacons [[tosn:Acts 6:2-6]].

7.s: Stephen retells Israel’s history, accusing the leaders of resisting the Holy Spirit. He sees Jesus standing at God’s right hand and is stoned, praying, “Lord, don’t hold this sin against them!” Saul approves.
7.d: Stephen sees Jesus standing at God’s right hand, though the Bible usually describes him as seated [[tosn:Acts 7:55-56]]. His dying prayer, “Lord, don’t hold this sin against them!”, is much like Jesus’ prayer on the cross [[tosn:Acts 7:59-60]] [[bible:Acts 7:60]]. He is the first Christian martyr [[tbd:016:Paul the Apostle]].

8.s: Persecution scatters the believers. Philip preaches in Samaria, and later explains Isaiah 53 to an Ethiopian official, who is baptized.
8.d: Scattered by persecution, the believers spread the good news through Judea and Samaria [[bsn:Acts 8:1-8]], as Acts 1:8 foretold [[tosn:Acts 1:8]]. Philip’s meeting with the Ethiopian official shows the good news is for all people, whatever their background [[tosn:Acts 8:26-40]].

9.s: On the road to Damascus Saul is blinded by a light and hears Jesus: “Saul, why do you persecute me?” Ananias lays hands on him. Peter heals Aeneas and raises Tabitha.
9.d: Saul’s conversion is so central that Luke tells it three times (chapters 9, 22 and 26) [[tosn:Acts 9:1-19]]. Barnabas convinces the apostles that it is real [[tosn:Acts 9:26-28]]. Christianity is called “the Way” [[tosn:Acts 9:2]].

10.s: Peter sees a vision of unclean animals: “What God has cleansed, you must not call unclean.” He visits the Roman centurion Cornelius, and the Spirit falls on Gentiles.
10.d: Cornelius was a God-fearing Gentile, one of those who admired Judaism and worshipped God [[tosn:Acts 10:2]]. “God doesn’t show favoritism” [[bible:Acts 10:34]] [[tosn:Acts 10:34-35]]: Peter sees that God accepts Gentiles as he accepts Jews who trust in Jesus [[tosn:Acts 11:4-17]].

11.s: Peter explains to Jerusalem what happened. In Antioch many Greeks believe, and the disciples are first called “Christians”.
11.d: Jews traditionally did not eat with Gentiles, but the church in Jerusalem learns that God has given them his word too [[tosn:Acts 11:1-18]]. In Antioch many Gentiles believe, and Saul begins his work among them there [[bsn:Acts 11:19-30]] [[tosn:Acts 11:21-24]].

12.s: Herod Agrippa kills James and imprisons Peter, who is freed by an angel while the church prays. Herod dies.
12.d: God sets Peter free [[bsn:Acts 12:1-17]]. Herod Agrippa I, who accepted the people’s worship, dies a painful death; the Jewish historian Josephus also describes it [[tosn:Acts 12:18-23]].

13.s: Barnabas and Saul are sent out from Antioch on the first missionary journey. In Pisidian Antioch Paul preaches in the synagogue and turns to the Gentiles.
13.d: From here Luke calls him Paul, his Roman name, which may show that his mission to the Gentiles is now in view [[tosn:Acts 13:9]]. Paul starts in the synagogues, where both Jews and God-fearing Gentiles could hear the message [[tosn:Acts 13:5]].

14.s: In Iconium, Lystra and Derbe, Paul and Barnabas are mistaken for gods, then Paul is stoned and left for dead, but gets up and goes on.
14.d: The signs God did among Jews are done among Gentiles too [[tosn:Acts 14:8-20]], and the reports back give the glory to God’s work [[tosn:Acts 14:26-28]]. “Through many afflictions we must enter into God’s Kingdom” [[bible:Acts 14:22]].

15.s: The council at Jerusalem decides Gentile believers need not be circumcised or keep the whole law of Moses. Paul and Barnabas part ways over John Mark.
15.d: The first council of the church meets over whether Gentiles must be circumcised [[tosn:Acts 15:4-21]]. James, the brother of Jesus, shows from the prophets (Amos 9) that Gentiles should be welcomed as Gentiles, without extra rules [[tosn:Acts 15:13-19]] [[tosn:Acts 15:15-19]].

16.s: With Silas and Timothy, Paul is called in a vision to Macedonia. Lydia believes in Philippi; Paul and Silas are jailed, sing at midnight, and the jailer believes.
16.d: The shift from “they” to “we” suggests Luke now travelled with Paul [[tosn:Acts 16:10]] [[bsn:Acts 16:1-10]]. The good news reaches Macedonia, in Europe [[bsn:Acts 16:1-10]].

17.s: In Thessalonica and Berea, then in Athens, Paul speaks at the Areopagus about the “unknown god”, quoting Greek poets.
17.d: The Bereans examined the Scriptures daily [[bible:Acts 17:11]], good examples of eager, thoughtful listeners [[tosn:Acts 17:10-12]]. In Athens Paul speaks to people who did not know the Scriptures, quoting their own poets [[tosn:Acts 17:22-31]] [[bsn:Acts 17:16-34]].

18.s: In Corinth Paul stays eighteen months, making tents with Aquila and Priscilla. Apollos is taught the way of God more accurately.
18.d: An ancient inscription shows Gallio was governor of Achaia around AD 51–52, which helps date Paul’s time in Corinth [[tosn:Acts 18:12-13]]. Claudius had ordered the Jews to leave Rome around AD 49 [[tosn:Acts 18:2-3]].

19.s: In Ephesus Paul teaches for two years; magic books are burned; a riot breaks out led by silversmiths of Artemis.
19.d: Paul stays in Ephesus for more than two years [[tosn:Acts 18:23-19:41]]. Artemis was the city’s great goddess [[tosn:Acts 19:23-41]], and archaeologists have uncovered the theatre where the crowd gathered, which could hold about 24,000 people [[tosn:Acts 19:29]].

20.s: Paul travels through Macedonia and Greece. In Troas Eutychus falls from a window and is raised. Paul says farewell to the Ephesian elders: “It is more blessed to give than to receive.”
20.d: Paul quotes a saying of Jesus that is not in the Gospels: “It is more blessed to give than to receive” [[tosn:Acts 20:35]] [[bible:Acts 20:35]].

21.s: Paul goes to Jerusalem despite warnings, is attacked in the temple, and is arrested by the Romans.
21.d: Like the Old Testament prophets, Agabus acts out his message, binding Paul’s hands with his belt [[tosn:Acts 21:10]]. Paul is ready even to die for the Lord Jesus [[tosn:Acts 21:11-14]].

22.s: Paul tells the crowd his conversion story; when he mentions the Gentiles they riot. He is a Roman citizen and avoids flogging.
22.d: Paul tells his own people his story, from his training under Gamaliel to his meeting with Jesus [[tosn:Acts 22:1-21]].

23.s: Before the council Paul divides Pharisees and Sadducees over the resurrection. A plot is uncovered, and he is sent to the governor Felix in Caesarea.
23.d: Paul’s nephew foils a plot to kill him [[tosn:Acts 23:16-22]], and Jesus assures Paul, “so you must testify also at Rome” [[tosn:Acts 23:11]] [[bible:Acts 23:11]].

24.s: Paul defends himself before Felix, who keeps him in prison for two years, hoping for a bribe.
24.d: Felix, a notably corrupt governor, is terrified when Paul speaks of “righteousness, self-control, and the judgment to come” [[tosn:Acts 24:25]] [[bible:Acts 24:25]].

25.s: Before the new governor Festus, Paul appeals to Caesar. King Agrippa wants to hear him.
25.d: Paul appeals to Caesar [[tosn:Acts 25:10-11]], confirming that he must go to Rome [[tosn:Acts 25:12]].

26.s: Paul tells King Agrippa his story. Agrippa says, “With a little persuasion are you trying to make me a Christian?”
26.d: Paul says he is on trial only because he believes God has fulfilled Israel’s hope of the resurrection [[tosn:Acts 26:1-23]] [[bsn:Acts 26:1-32]].

27.s: Sailing to Rome, Paul’s ship is caught in a storm for two weeks. Paul encourages everyone, and all 276 people reach land safely when the ship wrecks.
27.d: This vivid account is one of the best descriptions of an ancient sea journey [[tosn:Acts 27:1-28:16]], and the 276 people on board fits what is known of grain ships of the time [[tosn:Acts 27:36-37]].

28.s: On Malta Paul survives a snakebite and heals many. In Rome he lives under house arrest for two years, “preaching God’s Kingdom… with all boldness, without hindrance.”
28.d: Under house arrest Paul preaches “without hindrance”, the last word of Acts in Greek [[tosn:Acts 28:31]]. Paul was later executed in Rome before Nero died in AD 68; tradition says he was beheaded on the Ostian Road [[tbd:016:Paul the Apostle]].
